en.title: Work on it for 10 minutes
en.summary: You don't need to finish it. Just start the smallest piece for 10 minutes.
steps: Pick the one task that's bothering you most.
Write down the very first physical step (e.g. 'open the document').
Set a 10-minute timer and do only that.
When the timer ends, you can stop — or keep going if you want.
en.why: Starting small can make a large task feel more manageable.

en.title: Split it into three steps
en.summary: Write the task as three smaller steps, and circle the easiest one.
steps: Write the task at the top of a page.
Break it into three smaller steps.
Circle the easiest one — that's your next move.
en.why: Seeing smaller pieces can reduce the feeling that everything has to happen at once.

en.title: Plan just tomorrow
en.summary: Choose the 2–3 things that matter most for tomorrow, and give each a time.
steps: List everything on your mind for 2 minutes.
Pick the 2–3 that matter most for tomorrow.
Give each one a realistic time slot.
Leave the rest on the list — it's safely written down.
en.why: A short, concrete plan can make a busy period feel more contained.

en.title: Prepare one answer out loud
en.summary: Pick one likely question and practise answering it out loud, once.
steps: Pick one question you're likely to be asked.
Write 3 bullet points you'd want to mention.
Say your answer out loud once — imperfect is fine.
Notice one thing you did well.
en.why: Practising one concrete thing can turn general worry into something you can act on.

en.title: One problem, three options
en.summary: Name the problem in one sentence, then write three possible next steps — even imperfect ones.
steps: Write the problem in one sentence.
List three possible next steps, without judging them.
Pick the one that's most doable this week.
Decide when you'll do the first part.
en.why: Writing options down can make a problem feel less stuck.

en.title: A 10-minute money snapshot
en.summary: Write down what's coming in and going out this month — just the big items.
steps: Write your expected income for this month.
List the 5 biggest expenses.
Mark one you could reduce or delay.
Note one person or service you could ask for advice.
en.why: Seeing the numbers can make money worry more specific and easier to plan around.

en.title: Slow breathing for 3 minutes
en.summary: Breathe in for 4 counts and out for 6 counts, for about 3 minutes.
steps: Sit or stand comfortably.
Breathe in gently through your nose for 4 counts.
Breathe out slowly for 6 counts.
Repeat for about 3 minutes. Stop if you feel dizzy.
en.why: A longer out-breath is commonly used to help the body settle.

en.title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
en.summary: Notice 5 things you see, 4 you can touch, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste.
steps: Name 5 things you can see.
Name 4 things you can touch.
Name 3 things you can hear.
Name 2 things you can smell.
Name 1 thing you can taste.
en.why: Focusing on your senses can bring attention back to the present moment.

en.title: Set a 10-minute worry window
en.summary: Write every worry down for 10 minutes, then close the notebook until tomorrow.
steps: Set a 10-minute timer.
Write down every worry, without solving them.
Star any that you can act on.
Close the notebook. If a worry returns later, remind yourself it's written down.
en.why: Putting worries on paper can make them feel less like they need attention all day.

en.title: A 20-minute wind-down tonight
en.summary: Put your phone away 20 minutes before bed and do something calm instead.
steps: Pick a time to start winding down tonight.
Put your phone out of reach, or on another side of the room.
Do something calm: read, stretch, or listen to quiet music.
If you can't sleep after a while, get up briefly and do something calm before trying again.
en.why: A consistent wind-down is a common part of healthy sleep routines.

en.title: Choose a wake-up time
en.summary: Pick one wake-up time you can keep for the next 3 days, including weekends.
steps: Choose a realistic wake-up time.
Set an alarm for it for the next 3 days.
Get some daylight soon after waking if you can.
Notice how you feel after 3 days.
en.why: A steady wake-up time is often suggested as a foundation for better sleep.

en.title: A 15-minute offline break
en.summary: Log out of one app for 15 minutes and do something with your hands or body.
steps: Pick the app you open most without thinking.
Log out or move it off your home screen for now.
Spend 15 minutes on something offline: a walk, tidying, cooking, music.
Notice how you feel afterwards.
en.why: Short breaks can make it easier to notice how scrolling affects your mood.

en.title: A 10-minute walk
en.summary: Step outside, or walk around inside, for 10 minutes. No goal other than moving.
steps: Put on shoes.
Walk for 10 minutes — outside if you can.
Notice three things around you while walking.
That's it. Getting started was the hard part.
en.why: Small amounts of activity are often linked with small lifts in mood and energy.

en.title: Do one small thing you usually enjoy
en.summary: Pick something small you used to enjoy and do it for 15 minutes, even if you don't feel like it.
steps: List three small things you've enjoyed before.
Pick the easiest one.
Do it for 15 minutes.
Rate your mood before and after, out of 10.
en.why: Doing small enjoyable things — before motivation arrives — can gently lift mood.

en.title: Send one message
en.summary: Send a short message to one person you feel comfortable with. It can be simple.
steps: Think of one person you feel okay talking to.
Send something simple: 'Hey, thinking of you — how's it going?'
You don't need to explain how you feel unless you want to.
en.why: Small moments of connection can matter, even when they feel minor.

en.title: Talk it through with someone you trust
en.summary: Think of one person you trust and plan when you could talk to them this week.
steps: Think of someone who usually listens well.
Decide what you'd like to share — even one sentence.
Choose a time this week to call, meet, or message them.
If no one comes to mind, that's okay — a counsellor or helpline can also listen.
en.why: Sharing what's on your mind can make it feel lighter and less isolating.

en.title: Prepare what you want to say
en.summary: Write one sentence about how you feel and one about what you'd like, before a difficult conversation.
steps: Write: 'I feel ___ when ___.'
Write: 'What I'd like is ___.'
Choose a calm moment to talk, if it feels safe.
It's okay to take a break if the conversation gets heated.
en.why: Clear, calm 'I' statements can make difficult conversations easier.

en.title: Talk to yourself like a friend
en.summary: Write what you'd say to a friend in your situation — then read it as if it were for you.
steps: Imagine a friend is going through exactly this.
Write 2–3 sentences you'd say to them.
Read them back slowly, as if they were meant for you.
en.why: Many people are much kinder to friends than to themselves; this flips that around.

en.title: What matters to you here?
en.summary: Write down what you care about in this situation, and one small step towards it.
steps: Write down the situation in a sentence.
Ask: what do I care about here? (e.g. learning, honesty, family, growth)
Pick one small action this week that fits that value.
en.why: Connecting choices to what matters to you can make uncertainty easier to navigate.

en.title: Three-line reflection
en.summary: Write what happened, how it felt, and one thing you need right now.
steps: What happened today? (one line)
How did it feel? (one line)
What's one thing I need right now? (one line)
en.why: Putting feelings into words can make them feel more manageable.

en.title: Notice how stress shows up
en.summary: Spend 3 minutes noticing where stress shows up in your body and thoughts — no need to change it.
steps: Notice your body: shoulders, jaw, stomach, breathing.
Notice your thoughts: are they racing, repeating, or planning?
Name it: 'This is stress showing up.'
Notice whether naming it changes anything, even slightly.
en.why: Recognising your own stress signals can help you respond to them earlier.

en.title: Release tension, one area at a time
en.summary: Gently tense and relax your shoulders, hands and face, one at a time.
steps: Tense your shoulders for 5 seconds, then let them drop.
Make fists for 5 seconds, then relax your hands.
Scrunch your face for 5 seconds, then soften it.
Take one slow breath and notice the difference.
en.why: Alternating tension and release is a common relaxation technique.

en.title: Consider talking to a professional
en.summary: If this has been going on for a while, a doctor, counsellor or mental health professional could help. Let's think about one way to reach out.
steps: Think about who you could contact: a college counsellor, a doctor, or a helpline.
Write down what you'd like to tell them — even a few words.
Choose a day this week to reach out.
You can see the support options in the Support section.
en.why: A professional can help you understand what's going on and what support could fit.
